query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperature accelerates degradation because mechanical wear disrupts the naturally forming protective oxide films. This exposes dissimilar phases that, due to differences in their electrochemical potentials, form micro-galvanic cells that enhance localized corrosion. The combined action of mechanically induced oxide removal and galvanic corrosion leads to a synergistic increase in overall material loss.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting distinct phases (e.g., BCC and FCC or other intermetallic constituents) with pre-existing, thermally formed protective oxide layers at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or reciprocating contact) and exposure to a corrosive medium under elevated temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (for example, in the range of 450–650°C) under a corrosive environment (such as a molten salt or acidic atmosphere) along with an imposed wear cycle that intermittently removes or damages the oxide layers.
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries and the disrupted oxide film that normally protects the underlying phases, which then serve as sites for micro-galvanic coupling.
generation.mechanism: Wear-induced removal of the protective oxide exposes anodic (less corrosion-resistant) regions. Under elevated temperatures, the increased reaction kinetics and the inherent potential differences between adjacent phases promote galvanic corrosion at these interfaces, thereby accelerating overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Total degradation (material loss) will be significantly increased compared to the baseline of isolated wear or corrosion. Both the wear rate and corrosion rate will be enhanced, with the removal of protective oxides leading to a synergistic effect in the combined exposure case.
generation.baseline: Performance of the alloy under wear-only conditions and corrosion-only conditions at identical elevated temperatures, where degradation rates are lower and no significant synergistic interaction is observed.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected under conditions where the alloy forms a thermally activated oxide (without additional stabilization) and the microstructure comprises dissimilar phases that can establish galvanic couples. A single-phase alloy or one with a deliberately stabilized oxide would likely not exhibit the same synergistic acceleration.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of wear versus corrosion to the overall degradation acceleration is uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy composition, microstructural details, and test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the multi-phase eutectic HEA and subject them to: (1) wear-only (using a tribometer) at elevated temperature, (2) corrosion-only (via immersion/electrochemical cell) at the same temperature, and (3) simultaneous wear-corrosion. Characterize weight loss, surface oxide integrity, and electrochemical potential differences across phases (using techniques such as SEM, XPS, and scanning Kelvin probe microscopy).
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide layer integrity
Electrochemical potential mapping at phase interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation (weight loss, oxide disruption, and surface damage) observed in the simultaneous wear-corrosion test is not greater than the sum of the degradation from the separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests (i.e., if no synergistic effect is detected), or if no evidence of micro-galvanic coupling (differential potentials at phase boundaries) is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
